sections.label: GRC system introduced 1988
sections.summary: The GRC system was introduced in 1988 when the Parliamentary Elections Act and Constitution were amended to create three-Member GRCs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Group Representation Constituency (GRC) system was introduced in 1988 when the Parliamentary Elections Act and the Constitution were amended to provide for the creation of three-Member GRCs.

sections.label: 1991 GRC size changes
sections.summary: In 1991 the maximum GRC size rose from three to four candidates and the MP range became 25% to 75%, with a minimum of eight SMC MPs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In 1991, the maximum size of GRCs was increased from three to four candidates, and the number of MPs in GRCs was raised to a range of 25% to 75%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The upper limit of 75% on MPs from GRCs was removed and replaced by a minimum of eight MPs from Single Member Constituencies (SMCs).

sections.label: GRC seat percentage rise
sections.summary: Legislative changes in 1988, 1991 and 1996 saw GRC seats rise from 48% in 1988 to 74% in 1991 to 89% in 1997.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The legislative changes on GRC done in three stages, in the years 1988, 1991 and 1996 saw the percentage of GRC seats rise from 48% in the General Election (GE) in 1988 to 74% in GE 1991 to 89% in 1997.

sections.label: GRC vacancies and resignations
sections.summary: With GRC seats at 85% of elected seats, a departing MP leaves an 85% chance of a vacant seat, including Jurong GRC and Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: With the GRC seats comprising 85% of all elected seats in Parliament, the departure of any MP has an 85% chance of the seat remaining vacant.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The latest vacancy will be arising in Jurong GRC due to Senior Minister Tharman's decision to contest in the Presidential Election.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The current President also resigned in 2017 as a PAP MP, leaving a vacant seat in Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC.

sections.label: NCMP scheme for minorities
sections.summary: The first alternative is an NCMP scheme for minorities, similar to the current NCMP scheme for Opposition candidates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The first alternative is a Non-Constituency Member of Parliament (NCMP) scheme for minorities, similar to the current NCMP scheme for Opposition candidates.

sections.label: PAP seats versus vote share
sections.summary: The PAP currently holds close to 90% of elected seats in Parliament even though its national vote share is about 60%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Currently, the PAP has close to 90% of the elected seats in Parliament even though its national vote share is about 60%.

sections.label: Germany and New Zealand electoral systems
sections.summary: Germany uses about 50% first-past-the-post seats and half proportional representation, while New Zealand uses about 60% and 40% respectively.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In Germany, approximately 50% of the seats are based on the first-past-the-post system and the other half on proportional representation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In New Zealand, approximately 60% of the seats are on first-past-the-post system and 40% on proportional representation.

sections.label: GRC system sub-optimal outcomes
sections.summary: The GRC system has produced sub-optimal outcomes including voters held to ransom, weaker candidates riding coat-tails, and unfilled vacancies leaving residents underserved and under-represented.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the GRC system has generated several sub-optimal outcomes such as voters being held to ransom to vote for Ministers, weaker candidates riding on stronger candidates' coat-tails to Parliament and unfilled vacancies leading to residents being underserved and under-represented.

sections.label: Purposes of GRC and Elected Presidency
sections.summary: The GRC system was meant to ensure a minimum level of minority representation, while the Elected Presidency was meant to safeguard past Reserves with a second key.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The GRC system was meant to ensure that there will always be a minimum level of minority representation in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Elected Presidency, on the other hand, was meant to safeguard our increasingly large past Reserves by creating a second key to the past Reserves that was independent of the elected Government.

sections.label: GRC maximum size expansion
sections.summary: From the 1997 General Election onwards, GRCs were expanded to a maximum of six members.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: GRCs were expanded to a maximum of six members from the 1997 General Election onwards.

sections.label: Opposition votes and elected seats
sections.summary: In the last election, the Opposition won 39% of votes but comprises only 11% of elected Members of Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In the last election, the Opposition won 39% of the votes, but we only comprise 11% of the elected Members in Parliament.

sections.label: Average GRC member numbers
sections.summary: The average number of Members of Parliament in a GRC decreased from 5.4 in 2006 to 4.65 in 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: As a result, the average number of Members of Parliament in a GRC has decreased from 5.4 in 2006, to 4.65 in 2020.

sections.label: Tightened private sector candidate criteria
sections.summary: The Constitutional Commission recommended raising the share capital criteria for private sector candidates from $100 million to $500 million.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Constitutional Commission also recommended that the criteria for private sector candidates should be tightened significantly – the share capital criteria raised from $100 million to $500 million.

sections.label: Tan Cheng Bock disqualification
sections.summary: The changes meant Dr Tan Cheng Bock could not stand in 2017 and was permanently disqualified by the share capital requirement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The changes meant that Dr Tan Cheng Bock not only could not stand in 2017 but would also be permanently disqualified from becoming President because of the share capital requirement for private sector candidates.

sections.label: Parliamentary supermajority of 90%
sections.summary: It has controlled a Parliamentary supermajority of 90% of the seats throughout this time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Yet, throughout this time, it has controlled a Parliamentary supermajority of 90% of the seats.

sections.label: Origins of GRC system
sections.summary: The 1988 original purpose of the GRC system was to guarantee minimum minority representation in Parliament through structural electoral change.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: To quickly touch on the origins of the GRC system – the slated original purpose in 1988 was to guarantee a minimum representation of minorities in Parliament through a structural change to the electoral system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This would eliminate the possibility, however remote, of a Parliament where all elected Members were from a single race.

sections.label: Proposals for minority representation
sections.summary: Various proposals for minority representation were considered, including non-elected minority Members and an Upper House, before landing on the GRC system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Various proposals were made on how to ensure minority representation in Parliament, including having non-elected minority Members – similar to what the PSP is now proposing – having an Upper House with Members elected to represent various ethnic, religious and linguistic groups; and having representation outrightly proportionate to the racial composition of Singapore – also similar to something that the PSP is proposing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Various models have been considered and, ultimately, we landed on the GRC system.

sections.label: No perfect electoral systems
sections.summary: None of these systems are perfect and each country must decide the most appropriate system for its own context.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In other words, none of these systems are perfect systems and each country must decide on what is the most appropriate system for its own social, political and often, geographic context.

sections.label: GRC minority representation objectives
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the PSP accepts that the GRC system achieved its original primary objectives, including minority representation without race issues in elections.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Second, does the PSP accept that the GRC system has achieved its original primary objectives?

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We have good minority representation in the House.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But more importantly, we have minority representation without concerns or issues of race being brought up during the elections.

sections.label: GRC system primary objective
sections.summary: The speaker says it is difficult to argue the GRC system has not met its primary objective of fuss-free minority representation in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In my view, it is difficult to argue that the GRC system has not met its primary objective and that is, to put it bluntly, to achieve fuss-free minority representation in Parliament, something that all the previous proposals may not have achieved.

sections.label: Abolishing GRC as gamble
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the PSP accepts that abolishing the GRC system is an experiment and a gamble risking national unity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Fifth, given all of the above, does the PSP therefore accept that abolishing the GRC system is an experiment?

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is a gamble for which if we lose, we stand to jeopardise the very unity of our country.

sections.label: Reducing GRC sizes, more SMCs
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the PSP accepts that reducing GRC sizes and increasing SMCs can satisfactorily ameliorate the GRC system's advantages while preserving them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: My final question is: does the PSP accept that the advantages of the GRC system can be ameliorated to a satisfactory extent by reducing the sizes of GRCs and increasing the number of SMCs, while at the same time, preserving its advantages?

sections.label: Government commitment on GRC sizes
sections.summary: The Government has already committed to reducing the sizes of GRCs and introducing more SMCs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Government has already committed to reducing the sizes of GRCs and introducing more SMCs.

sections.label: Lee replying to NMP Motion
sections.summary: Mr Lee was replying to a Motion by the NMP that included a call to move beyond race and treat everyone as equal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Mr Lee was replying to a Motion by the NMP that included a call to move beyond race and to treat everyone as equal.

sections.label: Opposition to abolishing GRC system
sections.summary: The speaker quotes Mr Lee's remarks on realism and says he will not support the Motion to abolish the GRC system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In response to that the NMP's call that all are equal and should be treated equally, Mr Lee said, and I quote, "It is not reality, it is not practical, it will lead to grave and irreparable damage if we work on that principle." He went on to say, "The way that Singapore has made progress is by a realistic step-by-step forward approach." He ended his speech by saying, "Perhaps, I should bring this House back to earth and remind everybody what is our starting point, what is our base and if we do not recognise where we started from and that these are our foundations, we will fail." So, let us be realistic and make decisions not on aspiration or idealism.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This Motion invites this House to embark on an experiment; a perpetual experiment if we abolish the GRC system, which we will have to head into every future election with and with every future candidate and every future contesting party must contend with.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It is Singapore that loses and it is our fellow Singaporeans who will lose.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And it is in this regard that I will not support the Motion.

sections.label: Reducing GRC size and area
sections.summary: The speaker proposes reducing the maximum number of individuals and the area covered by a GRC, and increasing SMCs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, I would like to propose reducing the maximum number of individuals allowed in a GRC, reducing the area or boundaries covered by a GRC, and increasing the number of SMCs.

sections.label: More seats through SMCs
sections.summary: The speaker proposes that more seats be made available in Parliament through SMCs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Second, I would like to propose that more seats be made available in Parliament through SMCs.

sections.label: Female representative in each GRC
sections.summary: The speaker proposes mandating at least one female representative in the GRC to increase female Parliamentarians and diverse discussions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Mandating having at least one female representative in the GRC would increase the number of female Parliamentarians, adding to the diverse discussions and debates here.

sections.label: Addressing Hazel Poa's coat-tailing view
sections.summary: The speaker addresses Hazel Poa's view that GRCs can let popular MPs carry less popular ones into Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: At this juncture, I would like to address a view shared by hon Member Hazel Poa that GRCs have the potential to enable more popular MPs to carry less popular ones into Parliament, or coat-tailing.

sections.label: Public submissions on multiracial Parliament
sections.summary: The Committee received submissions: 81% supporting a multiracial Parliament, 52% supporting the GRC scheme, and 29% supporting other concepts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Committee received public submissions, 81% supporting the need to ensure a multiracial Parliament, 52% supporting to achieve it with the GRC scheme and 29% supporting the need to ensure a multiracial Parliament but with concepts other than the GRC, which were some of those examples I gave earlier.

sections.label: Minority MPs in Parliament
sections.summary: The Bill passed in 1988; in 2023, 28.3% of elected MPs are from minority communities, excluding NMPs and NCMPs, versus 19.5% in 1987.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Bill was passed in Parliament on 18 May 1988.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Today in Parliament, in 2023, we have 28.3% of all elected MPs in Parliament, excluding NMPs and NCMPs who are from minority communities as compared to 19.5% back in 1987.

sections.label: GRC effect on opposition
sections.summary: An IPS article states GRC's winner-takes-all effect does not disadvantage credible opposition and can knock out an entire PAP team, as in Aljunied GRC in 2011.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As published in an Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) article in 2013, “In fact, the winner-takes-all effect of GRC does not disadvantage credible opposition but in fact, GRC also advantages the opposition, as it can knock out an entire team of PAP candidates in one constituency, as it did in Aljunied GRC in 2011, when the Workers' Party dislodged the PAP slate consisting of three political officeholders and one newbie touted as a future Minister.” I believe the "newbie" made it.

sections.label: Last speech on matter
sections.summary: The speaker says this is their last speech in Parliament on such a matter, likening it to poisoning Singapore and causing self-harm as a nation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I cannot believe I am making my last speech in Parliament on such a matter.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This is likened to poisoning our own body, that is, Singapore our country and our home, and causing self-harm to ourselves as a nation.

sections.label: Good leaders and harmony
sections.summary: The speaker says politics can feel thankless and subject to scrutiny, and that good leaders are needed to serve Singaporeans and guard multiracial harmony.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: At the same time, it is political, and those involved can oftentimes feel like it is a thankless job, one that is subject to public scrutiny and even unscrupulous character assassination at the will of dirty politics.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: To ensure that our Parliament continues to govern well, we will need good leaders to step forward, to serve Singaporeans, to do it out of love for Singapore, for the common good for all in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Singapore is a multiracial, multi-religious society not by chance and we need to guard our multiracial harmony very carefully.

sections.label: GRC system and racial representation
sections.summary: The speaker says the GRC system reflects the priority that law-making power rests with representatives from all races, and Singapore will not be fractured along racial lines.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: At the end of the day, though, whilst the system is not perfect, the GRC system does reflect the single most important priority for Singaporeans – that the highest law-making power of our land rests in the hands of representatives from all races in order that the way we order our society reflects the interests of all.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Singapore cannot and will not be fractured along racial lines, not just because we ensure that there is an adequate number of elected representatives from minority races but also because the way we do so refuses to allow politics to be conducted on racial lines.

sections.label: Motion to abolish GRC
sections.summary: The speaker says the Motion calls for abolishing the GRC system, which would be irresponsible, and calls the GRC system underrated and a paradox.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: But what is noteworthy is that this Motion calls for this House to abolish the GRC system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It would be irresponsible for this House to abolish the GRC system and then consider what should be the system to replace it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The GRC system, to me, is a most underrated structure in giving Singapore politics its unique character.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It is a paradox that both elevates race and takes away its sting.

sections.label: Elected MP for Bukit Batok
sections.summary: The speaker was returned as MP for Bukit Batok again with a reduced majority, elected twice as a minority-race MP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In the result, I was fortunate to be returned as MP for Bukit Batok once again, albeit with a reduced majority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: To be elected twice as an MP from a minority race in Bukit Batok SMC is certainly one of the high points in my life.

sections.label: Racial politicisation in campaigns
sections.summary: In 2016 the Prime Minister spoke out against online comments asking Chinese voters to vote along racial lines; in 2020 racial politicisation continued.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In the first campaign in 2016, the situation was concerning enough for Prime Minister Lee, as the Secretary-General of the PAP, to speak out against online comments and whispers that went around Bukit Batok asking Chinese voters to cast their ballots along racial lines on 30 April 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In the second campaign in 2020, I continued to encounter politicisation along racial lines.

sections.label: Graffiti about speaker's Indianness
sections.summary: The graffiti was an attempt to make the speaker even more Indian, as if his name and skin colour were too understated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The graffiti was an attempt to make me even more Indian, as if my name and skin colour were too understated.

sections.label: Winning SMC and GRC system
sections.summary: Winning two elections in an SMC does not provide grounds to do away with the GRC system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The fact that I won two elections in an SMC does not provide grounds to do away with the GRC system.

sections.label: Abolishing GRC and minority candidates
sections.summary: If the GRC system is abolished, good people from minority races may decide not to run for elections.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: If the GRC system is abolished, we will have to contend with the scenario that good people from minority races, knowing that there is a danger of elections being politicised along racial lines, may just decide this is too much trouble and not run for elections.

sections.label: Need for the GRC
sections.summary: Until that day, the GRC will still be needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: Until that day, we will still need the GRC.

sections.label: Motion to abolish GRCs
sections.summary: The Motion before the House calls for the GRC system to be abolished altogether, not reformed.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: But let me first address the Motion put before us, because this is not a Motion for reforming GRCs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: This is a Motion that calls for the GRC system to be abolished altogether.

sections.label: GRC system multiracial guarantees
sections.summary: The GRC system guarantees a multiracial Parliament and requires multiracial teams, pushing parties toward moderate campaigning.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: Our GRC system guarantees that Parliament will always be multiracial and representative of the make-up of our society.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: Next, because the GRC system requires constituencies to be contested by multiracial teams of candidates, political parties and their candidates have to take a moderate, multiracial approach when campaigning instead of a communal or racially extreme approach.

sections.label: GRC sizes and EBRC boundaries
sections.summary: Average GRC size has fallen and SMC numbers risen, and the EBRC will consider various factors to decide boundaries.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: As Members have pointed out, the average size of the GRC has come down and the number of SMCs has gone up in the last two elections.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: Ultimately, the EBRC will take into consideration various factors, including what was mentioned today, to decide on the boundaries.

sections.label: Opposition numbers after 2020 GE
sections.summary: After the 2020 GE there are 10 Opposition Members and two NCMPs, with numbers depending more on candidate quality.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: After the 2020 GE, we now have 10 Opposition Members elected to this House as well as two NCMPs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: I think it would be fair to say that the number of Opposition Members in this House ultimately depends more on the quality of the candidates, and whether they are able to secure the support of the Singaporeans to be elected to Parliament, than just whether they are competing in a SMC or GRC.

sections.label: Proportional representation race parties
sections.summary: A proportional representation system will in essence result in parties based on race, religion or special interest.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: In essence, a proportional representation system will result in parties based on race and religion, or a special interest.

sections.label: Poa's system racial division
sections.summary: Ms Poa's proposed system would bring in best-performing unsuccessful minority candidates, likely dividing Parliament along racial lines.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: If that is the case, Ms Poa's proposed system will then bring in the unsuccessful minority candidates who performed the best.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: We would then be likely to have, as Mr Raj Joshua Thomas have pointed out, a predominantly Chinese party in power, with minority Members or NCMPs in the Opposition.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: Parliament would then be divided along racial lines.

sections.label: CNA IPS racial preference survey
sections.summary: A 2021 CNA and IPS survey found in-group preference, with respondents preferring racially similar people for many roles.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: More recently in 2021, a survey conducted by CNA and Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) found that there is still in-group preference with respondents preferring those who are racially similar to themselves for many roles.

sections.label: Minority soldiers wanted AWOL
sections.summary: On the first day of his command, at least five minority soldiers in his unit wanted to go AWOL.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: In one of my commands, on the first day of assumption of my command, a minority group of soldiers wanted to go absent without official leave (AWOL), at least five of them.

sections.label: Reported racial riot risk
sections.summary: While grieving his late father-in-law, he received a report that a racial riot could soon break out in his unit over alleged racial discrimination.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: As my family was grieving for the loss of my late father-in-law, I received a report that a racial riot could soon break out in my unit, because there were allegations that there had been racial discrimination, injustice, and unfairness in the unit.

sections.label: GRC system multiracial safeguard
sections.summary: The GRC system safeguards that each GRC has at least one minority candidate competing as a team, making Parliament multiracial.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: The GRC system is thus a safeguard to ensuring that every GRC will have at least one minority candidate competing as a team and as a result, Parliament is multiracial, and we do our best to take race and religion out of the contest.

sections.label: US Supreme Court affirmative action ruling
sections.summary: Last week the US Supreme Court struck down race-based affirmative action programmes in universities.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: Just last week, the US Supreme Court struck down race-based affirmative action programmes in universities.

sections.label: Opposing Motion on minority representation
sections.summary: Supporting the Motion goes against the founding philosophy of accounting for minority interests and risks inadequate multiracial representation in the highest legislative body.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: To support this Motion is to go against our founding philosophy of ensuring that the interests of our minority communities are accounted for.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: To support this Motion is to risk having no or inadequate multiracial representation in the highest legislative body of the land.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: To support this Motion is to leave to chance the emergence of racial politics and forgo our continued progress towards a system where race is not to be a determining factor in electoral contest.

sections.label: PAP opposes abolishing GRC
sections.summary: The PAP will vote against the Motion to abolish the GRC, saying it goes against nation-building since Independence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
sentences.text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, the PAP will vote against this Motion to abolish the GRC because it fundamentally goes against what we have been trying to do in building our country as a nation that we can be all proud of for all these years since our Independence.

sections.label: No defence against gerrymandering claim
sections.summary: The speaker says PAP and NMP speeches did not defend the argument that the GRC system is used for gerrymandering, citing Fengshan and Joo Chiat.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In all the speeches from the PAP Members of Parliament and the Nominated Members of Parliament, I did not hear a defence to the argument that the GRC system is ridden on for gerrymandering purposes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: There was no convincing argument to me why Fengshan comes out when it is a tight SMC, Joo Chiat is included into a GRC when it is a tight SMC in previous elections.

sections.label: GRC as political football
sections.summary: The speaker agrees with Minister Chan on multiracial society but says the GRC system has become a political football, citing Mr Low Thia Khiang in 1996.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I take the points that Minister Chan made, and I think he made them respectfully; and respectfully, I agree with the fundamental issues with regard to a multiracial society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But when the GRC system becomes a political football, as it has been and, as Mr Low Thia Khiang also pointed out in 1996 when the size of GRCs increased to six, he put up a table in this House showing how the tight SMCs inevitably or invariably become GRCs, making it more difficult for the Opposition.

sections.label: Reserved Presidency shows alternatives
sections.summary: The speaker says the 2017 reserved Presidency shows the GRC is not a perfect system and other alternatives can be considered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Going by what has happened in 2017, when we introduced the reserved Presidency, I think it shows, indeed, the GRC is not a perfect system and there are other alternatives that can be considered.

sections.label: IPS survey on racial harmony
sections.summary: The speaker cites an IPS and onepeople.sg survey comparing 2018 and 2013 results, which found millennials more welcoming of racial diversity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I am sure the Minister would have also seen the IPS survey in conjunction with onepeople.sg, on the indicators of racial and religious harmony, comparing survey results from 2018 and 2013.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is not a perfect survey set, for sure, but this is what it says: "Analysing the results by respondents' age, millennials were found to be more welcoming of racial diversity." This is pulled out from page 52 from this IPS report.

sections.label: Multicultural values and GRC alternatives
sections.summary: The speaker says multicultural values are strong, concedes the GRC forces multiracial slates, but says other systems can ensure a racially balanced Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: These findings demonstrate a strong foothold of multicultural values in Singapore, with most Singaporeans internalising narratives of multiracialism and racial harmony." I do believe the GRC system had some part to play in this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I will concede that point because it forces Opposition parties to field a multiracial slate for the reasons the Minister mentioned.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: You are already going to be at the starting line without votes if you do not field a multiracial slate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But the reason why I pulled out these quotes was to put into perspective with respect Member Murali's experiences and some of the issues that the Minister raised to just provide a balance to some of the arguments on race and religion issues.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But fundamentally, there are systems out there which can accommodate, in my view, a racially balanced Parliament and, more fundamentally, with regard to the first issue, we need to understand where does the Minister stand on how the GRC system has been employed in the past.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: First, as I have said, today's Motion is to abolish the GRC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: Because to abolish the GRC, then what do we put in place to safeguard multiracial representation in Parliament?

sections.label: Vote on abolishing GRC
sections.summary: The speaker says the vote on this Motion hinges on whether to abolish the GRC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: So, we can continue to discuss how we can evolve the systems and what are the executional issues.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: But today, the vote on this Motion hinges on this: to abolish the GRC.

sections.label: Other countries' experiences
sections.summary: The speaker says other countries have spent over a hundred years on this issue without reaching near Singapore's system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: But we are also under no illusion that this is a job done.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: And if I may look at the experiences of other countries, some countries have spent hundred over years trying to overcome this issue and they have not achieved anywhere near even our own system.

sections.label: Minority representation in Parliament
sections.summary: The speaker says the Motion is moved with understanding and support for adequate minority representation in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: We come to this House for this Motion having the full understanding and support that we need adequate minority representation in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: That is the reason why in GE2020, we fielded 33% of our candidates from the minority group.

sections.label: Alternatives to GRC system
sections.summary: PSP says the NCMP scheme or modified proportional representation scheme would be a better alternative than the GRC system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: PSP has no monopoly over all the ideas.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: But we are quite confident that either the NCMP scheme or the modified proportional representation scheme will be a better alternative than the GRC system.

sections.label: GRC scheme reasons
sections.summary: The speaker says the introduction of a GRC scheme is not just due to minority representation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: What I mean is that the introduction of a GRC scheme is not just due to the minority representation.

sections.label: Singaporeans' perception of GRC
sections.summary: The speaker says many Singaporeans think the GRC system was not introduced just because of minority representation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The perception or the understanding of many Singaporeans is that they think that the GRC system was not introduced just because of the minority representation.

sections.label: Party seats and NCMPs
sections.summary: The speaker says allocating seats on party votes or lines encourages sectoral campaigning, and losing Opposition MPs as NCMPs could leave most minorities as NCMPs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: In fact, the experience of other countries, if we may be frank, is that when seats are allocated on party votes or party lines, it is a recipe for people to campaign precisely on the sectoral interest that we hope not to see.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: If seats are given to losing Opposition MPs to be NCMPs, then, I have just explained, we will end up in a House with a dominant party with the racial majority and then all our minorities are possibly, if all, if not, most of the minorities, will end up as NCMPs.

sections.label: Alternative proposals and integration
sections.summary: The speaker says the two alternative proposals will not lead to a more integrated or cohesive Parliament and will end up contested on sectoral or racial lines.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: Unfortunately, respectfully, I cannot see how the two alternative proposals will lead to a more integrated Parliament, a more cohesive Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: It will end up with politics being contested on sectoral interests, if not, racial lines.

sections.label: EBRC boundary report detail
sections.summary: The speaker suggests the Government push the EBRC to produce a more detailed report when boundaries are redrawn, noting past reports ran 30 to 50 pages.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The second point on the EBRC, I think it will be helpful, at least, going forward, for the Government to put its weight and significant influence behind a proposal to the EBRC to please produce a more detailed report when boundaries are redrawn.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I think in the past, we had boundary reports which extended to 30 to 50 pages, explaining why boundaries were redrawn in particular ways.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The latest EBRC report, I think is in the single digits for the number of pages.

sections.label: GRC system and minority representation
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister, saying Mr Lee Kuan Yew's thinking then proves the GRC system is not just about minority representation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: My question to the Minister is that the thinking of Mr Lee Kuan Yew at that time is proof to the fact that the GRC system, at least the perception of many Singaporeans like myself, is not just due to minority representation.

sections.label: Democracy and future generations
sections.summary: The speaker says a biggest problem of democracy is ensuring voters do not just vote on this generation's interests but on future generations' interests, called the missing-voter problem.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: One of the biggest problems of democracy is this – how do we ensure that when everybody votes, they do not just vote on this generation's interests but on the future generations' interests?

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: This is what I have always called the missing-voter problem.

sections.label: Responsibility to future generations
sections.summary: The speaker says Parliament has a responsibility to every generation after, and Singapore must think for the future or will not be around for it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: As the highest legislative body in this country, we have a responsibility not just to this generation but to every generation that comes after.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: Because no democratic system, or very few governance systems, perhaps minus the monarchy, will think about two or three generations down, because they think that they will still be around.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: But for Singapore, if we do not think for the future and do not think that we will be around for the future, we will definitely not be around for the future.

sections.label: Singapore governance and resource stewardship
sections.summary: The passage states that Singapore's governance and resource management distinguish it, and hopes future leaders never assume a perfect or copyable system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: That is how we govern, and that is how we steward our resources – from the way we manage land to the way we manage resources – that is what distinguishes us.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: And I hope, long may it be, that whoever runs Singapore will always think about this and never assume that there is a perfect system, or that we can just copy someone else's system and we will be exceptional and distinguished.

sections.label: GRC minority representation percentages
sections.summary: The passage states the GRC system ensures about 12% Malay and 6% Indians and Others representation, and proposes mandating candidate percentages in SMCs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: This means that the GRC system currently ensures about 12% Malay and 6% Indians and Others representation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: We can therefore ensure minority representation by mandating that at least 50%, 12% and 6% of each political party's candidates running in SMCs must be from the Chinese, Malay, Indian or Other communities respectively.

sections.label: Proportional representation threshold range
sections.summary: The passage states that a common range for thresholds in countries practising proportional representation is around 4% to 5%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: A common range for thresholds in countries that practise the proportional representation system is around 4% to 5%.

sections.label: PAP vote and seat share
sections.summary: The passage states that PAP gets about 60% of the national vote but nearly 90% of the elected seats.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: As I have mentioned before, PAP gets about 60% of the national vote but nearly 90% of the elected seats.

sections.label: Vote share to seat share
sections.summary: The passage states that if 60% of the national vote gives 90% of seats, then 40% of the vote can give only 10% of seats.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: If 60% of the national vote translates into 90% of the elected seats; then, that means that a national vote share of 40% can result in only 10% of the seats.

sections.label: Minority MPs before and after GRCs
sections.summary: The passage states 16 minority MPs were elected in GE 1984, 20.3% of elected MPs, and 19.8% in GE 1988 after GRCs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: In GE 1984, before the introduction of GRCs, 16 minority MPs were elected, making up 20.3% of all elected Members of Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: After the introduction of GRCs, in GE 1988, minority Members of Parliament made up 19.8% of all elected Members of Parliament, a slight drop compared to GE 1984.

sections.label: Uncontested seats after GRC changes
sections.summary: In GE1988 uncontested seats were 13.6%, then rose to 50.6% and 56.6% in GEs 1991 and 1997 after GRC sizes increased.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: In GE1988, the percentage of uncontested seats dropped to 13.6%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: However, in the next two GEs, after the GRC sizes were further increased, uncontested seats jumped from 13.6% to 50.6% and 56.6% in GEs 1991 and 1997 respectively.

sections.label: Minority representation or political advantage
sections.summary: It asks whether the measure was for minority representation or political advantage, noting minorities rose to 28% of elected MPs in GE2020 without further intervention.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: Was it truly for minority representation or was it for political advantage?

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: It is worth noting that in GE 2020, without any further intervention to help minority candidates, the percentage of elected MPs who are minorities has increased to 28%.

sections.label: Parliament lawmaker, Court executes laws
sections.summary: It states Parliament is the lawmaker and the Court executes laws made by Parliament, which it says puts the cart before the horse.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: Considering that Parliament is the lawmaker, the Court executes the laws made by Parliament, I think this rather puts the cart before the horse.

sections.label: Single-party system entrenching power
sections.summary: It says moving ahead swiftly needs strong political leadership, but without regular leadership turnover and political competition a single-party system risks entrenching power in a small group.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: We could move ahead swiftly, with strong political leadership.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: However, without the regular turnover of leadership and political competition, a single-party system also carries the risk of entrenching power within a small group.

sections.label: Call to abolish GRCs
sections.summary: It urges all Members and Singaporeans to support abolishing GRCs and to consider alternative ways of ensuring minority representation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: One of these is to abolish the GRC.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: I urge all Members and Singaporeans to support the call to abolish GRCs and consider alternative ways of ensuring minority representation.

sections.label: No guarantee of minority MPs
sections.summary: It says mathematically, unless each minority candidate competes in the same SMC, there is no guarantee that parties having many minorities will yield so many minorities in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: Mathematically, unless each of the minority candidate compete in the same SMC, as you proposed, there is no guarantee that just because Party A, B, or C have so many minorities, we will end up with so many minorities in the Parliament.

sections.label: Racial slate and multiracial outcome
sections.summary: A racial slate does not guarantee the multiracial Parliament representation that is desired.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: Just because people have a slate according to racial profile does not guarantee that the outcome will be a multiracial representation of the Parliament that we so desire.

sections.label: Single issue versus holistic voting
sections.summary: It asks whether electoral politics should be single issue outcomes or a matured electorate considering all challenges holistically.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: It could be race or religion, or it could be green issues, as the Member mentioned.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
sentences.text: But the question for us is this – even if we consider this seriously, do we want our electoral politics where people vote on single issue outcomes, or do we want a matured electorate that we are progressing towards, where people holistically consider all the challenges facing our country?

sections.label: Party list racial representation selection
sections.summary: Party list candidates are chosen to meet racial representation requirements first, not strictly in order.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: The party list will have multi-racial candidates listed and each party, in the way that it chooses from the party list, is not strictly in order, like as in other countries, but to be chosen in such a way to meet racial representation requirements first.

sections.label: Racial abuse and minority representation
sections.summary: It asks whether minority candidates must accept racial abuse rather than a system reducing abuse while allowing minority representation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Does that imply that she is asking minority candidates and future minority candidates to accept such racial abuse, because it may not matter and because he may win in elections, rather than having a system that prevents or at least reduces the probability of the minority candidate from being subjected to such abuse and yet, at the same time, allows the minority representation in Parliament, because we show up together as a multiracial team?

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: I am not suggesting that minority candidates should just accept those treatment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: I am suggesting racism be tackled holistically for the whole society because it is not only election candidates who encounter such incidents.
